Curators Comments:
South Asian Heritage Month is the name given to the month-long celebration in the South Asian diaspora to celebrate the heritage of people with roots in the South Asian countries of India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives. The South Asian community in the UK organised the concept launch of the first South Asian Heritage Month event in July 2019 at the House of Commons. The first South Asian Heritage Month took place in 2020.
South Asian Heritage Month runs from 18 July to 17 August and seeks to commemorate, mark and celebrate South Asian cultures, histories, particularly the intertwined histories of the UK and South Asian communities and how South Asian cultures are present throughout the UK.

Description: A sheep's carrying bag, woven; made of yak hair.  Used to transport salt.;
Curators Comments:
Text from Eth Doc 1882: [Susi Dunsmore] Caravans of sheep ...
     Ang Diku Sherpa bought this bag in West Nepal in 1993: the maker and the age of the bag are unknown.  Caravans of sheep and goats using this type of bag can still be seen in some northern parts of Nepal.  This bag is woven from Yak hair, single yarn for warp and weft in a warpfaced plain weave.
     12cm wide leather strips strengthen the bottom of the bag.
     Cotton cloth is stitched underneath the bag to act as padding.  The ropes are made of two 4 ply strands stitched together.
     When the bag pockets are filled, they are closed by stitching with a strand of 2-ply yarn.
     [Ang Diku Sherpa]  Some strong sheep carry double.  Sheep bag makers mostly those who have yak.  The blacksmith from Jumla [from whom Ang Diku bought the bag said bags such as this were] made by Tibetan women from Humla, Dolpo, Jumla and Manang.  [This bag was] made by Humla women [he believed].  East Nepal [stopped] making that type of bag since long time.  I remember used to be.  Now no more.  Some men and women from Changchung Gola they make just rope and floor carpet and bag for yak to carry, not sheep bag.
Acq notes (acq): Text from Eth Doc 1882: Ang Diku Sherpa bought this bag in from the blacksmith in Jumla, west Nepal in 1993.  The maker and the age of the bag are unknown.

Description: A bronze Ghanta or handbell curved with a female head in the middle, paired with a vajra (1948,0716.11.b), stored with this object in a red leather covered container.;
Curators Comments:
Zwalf 1985
The ‘vajra’ and ‘ghaṇṭā’ were the most important ritual implements of Vajrayāna Buddhism. The ‘vajra’, symbolising the unbreakable Absolute, hardly survives as a ritual object from Buddhist India but is found in Indonesia, Nepal, Tibet and Japan. Paired with the bell, it symbolised compassion or the 'male' skill in means for salvation; the bell was the symbol of supreme knowledge seen as female. Together they constituted a unity of coefficients for salvation. Held in the right and left hands respectively to make elaborate ritual movements, they are also the attributes of many deities.

Description: Cast, copper alloy signet-ring with a flat, oval bezel, joined at the shoulders to the rounded ends of the (broken) shank. WIthin a dotted border is the engraved motif of a 'vase of plenty' (purnaghata) with four incised lines above indicating foliage. The simplified oblique lines on either side of the vase derive from the depiction of tendrils signifying growth and fruitfulness, but here seem to represent diadem ribbons.;
Dimensions: 15.60 millimetres bezel ;  22.90 millimetres;  11.30 millimetres bezel ;  4.60 millimetres shank ;
Curators Comments:
For documentation of IM.Metal.141 see 1880.3702.a. For other examples of the purnagatha motif, see 1880.3790.p–q, IOLC.7565, IOLC.7772 and seal 1880.3626.
C. Fabrègues: The purnaghata or purnakalasa (vase of plenty) is a common motif in Hindu, Jain and Buddhist art. It is one of the eight Indian astamangala (auspicious signs) symbolising abundance, like the cornucopia in Greek and Roman art. Its use is attested from about the 1st century BC onwards. It occurs on the reverse of 7th-century Nepalese coins with Kuvera, god of wealth, on the obverse (Rhodes, Gabrisch and Valdettaro 1989 p.45–7, pls.8–9), and survives in the form of the Tibetan bumpa (urn of wisdom) and in Hindu kumbha rituals. It is particularly prevalent in early Buddhist art, occurring on 1st-century BC–1st-century AD reliefs from Bharhut, Sanchi, Mathura and Amaravati; on 2nd-century reliefs from Nagarjunakonda and Anuradhapura; and on 1st–2nd-century Gandharan reliefs from Swat and the Peshawar Valley (Sivaramamurti 1974, fig.244; Marshall and Foucher 1947; Vogel 1930, pl.VII.15; Barrett 1954, pl.IX.29; Longhurst 1938, pl.31.c; Boisselier 1978, p.110, fig.24; Faccenna and Taddei 1964, vol.II.3, pl.DCXIV.a, WS.27; Tissot 1975, pl.XVI.8).
E. Errington: An identical bulbous vase with a long, narrow neck and lines emerging above a broad rim occurs on 6th-century Alchon Hun copper alloy coins found at Kashmir Smast in the Peshawar Valley (Nasim Khan, Errington and Cribb 2008, pp.89, 169, no.491). On the coins the flanking tendrils have also become ribbons, but are more realistically depicted. Earlier coins in the series and Alchon silver coins bearing the title ξαβοχο show a trident or three flowers instead of the ‘foliage’ lines (Nasim Khan, Errington and Cribb 2008, pp.89, 168, nos.489–90; Göbl 1967, pl.28.101).

Description: A rectangular wooden book cover painted on the inside face with a central figure of Prajñāparamitā flanked on each side by three rows of Bodhisattvas and monks; the outer face is carved with Buddhas.;
Curators Comments:
Probably the cover for a Prajnaparamita (Perfection of Wisdom) text.; Zwalf 1985
The wonderfully preserved painted face of this bookcover is its inner side; the outer, slightly convex, is carved with Buddhas. The style of painting derives from Nepal and eastern India, but the cover is Tibetan. The limited size of the oblong Indian and Nepalese palm-leaf pages was increased by the Tibetan use of paper, and wooden covers were correspondingly enlarged. The central deity is Prajñāpāramitā, or the Perfection of Wisdom, representing a central conception of Mahāyāna Buddhism, and the cover may have belonged to a Perfection of Wisdom text. The figures beside the goddess are Bodhisattvas and monks; the latter include what look like portraits of living or recent teachers whom it may be possible to recognise from other sources.
Bib references: Zwalf 1981 / Heritage of Tibet; Zwalf 1985 / Buddhism: Art and Faith

Curators Comments:
The donor's grandmother was a singer with the D'Olyly Carte opera company which was touring in the far east (according to the donor she was 19 at the time). During that tour the captain of the ship they were on proposed marriage to her and she declined. The donor did not know, but presumably she must have been given the coin (a 1799 Nepalese gold coin which has been mounted as jewelry) because preserved with the coin was a hand written note signed by Rakhal das Banerji (the spelling on the note differs but as was not uncommon at the time he wrote his name with several different spellings in Latin script, so I'm fairly confident about who it is, and recognised the name when I was shown it). He primarily worked for the Archaeological Survey of India, and is best known for his excavation of Mohenjo Daro (and thus, effectively, the discovery of the Indus Valley civilization). He only worked at the Calcutta Museum very briefly before the first world war, and so the note confirmed the coin had left Nepal by that point, and making it likely it was a gift to the donor's grandmother during her time with the opera company.
According to the donor she returned to Europe after declining the marriage proposal, joined a convent, and discovered she was ill-suited to the religious life. At that point she wrote to the captain to ask if he might still be amenable to marriage (which, presumably happily for the two of them it was). However, the first world war broke out before they could be re-united. The donor believed her grandmother worked as a nurse with the religious order she had joined through the war and that her grandfather shipped war supplies, and they were not able to marry until after the war ended.  -- Robert Bracey, by email, 25 Sept 2023.; The coin was mounted to be worn as jewellery in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century.

Title: Visitation I
Description:
Seated figure with short hair wearing jeans and a blue shirt, right hand raised, looking up at a bird in flight, with criss-crossing glittering lines creating a cloud between them. 2007
Ink on Nepal paper with graphite, colour pencil, mica, glitter and collage;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription quoted: Signed and dated in pencil (lower right): ‘Kiki Smith 2007’.;
Curators Comments: This large-scale work on paper references traditional Christian images of the Annunciation, in which the Virgin Mary is visited by the angel Gabriel who tells her that she will give birth to the son of God. Christian imagery occurs frequently in the work of Smith, who was raised a Roman Catholic, as do images of nature, in particular birds, and female figures modelled on herself. This is one of three Visitation drawings of the same scale and format, with the bird in different positions, which were exhibited together in the touring exhibition ‘Kiki Smith: Her Home’ (also called ‘Kiki Smith: Her Memory’ and ‘Kiki Smith: Sojourn’) in 2008-10. ‘Visitation II’ (or ‘Visitation of the Bird II’) is now in the collection of the Fondation Louis Vuitton, Paris. The exhibition examined the lives of women artists and the Annunciation was used as a metaphor for a moment of creative inspiration.

Description: A seated figure of the goddess Vasudhara with 6-arms (clockwise): one hand makes the gesture of giving, the next holds a jewelled stalk, and the third is raised in salutation; on the right are a book, a stalk of rice and a bowl held in the lap. The right foot rests beside a pot of plenty. Made of gilt bronze inlaid with coloured stones.;
Curators Comments:
Zwalf 1985
The Indian texts describe Vasudhārā, goddess of abundance and consort of Jambhala, god of riches, as two- or six-armed. In Nepal a six-armed form makes an early appearance and shows few variations. In this example, reading clockwise, one hand makes the gesture of giving, the next holds a jewelled stalk, and the third is raised in salutation; on the right are a book, a stalk of rice and a bowl held in the lap. The right foot rests beside a pot of plenty.
Bib references: Koezuka (1994) / Masterpieces of Buddhist and Hindu Art from the British Museum; Zwalf 1985 / Buddhism: Art and Faith

Description: An schist image of the Buddha standing, with his right hand in varadamudra and his left holding the end of his robe; at his feet is a kneeling devotee; inscribed.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: On the smooth front face of the base. Inscription language: Sanskrit Inscription script: Siddhamātrkā Inscription note: A three-line inscription names several donors who dedicate the merit from commissioning this image to the attainment of supreme knowledge (i.e. Buddhahood) by their teachers, kinsfolk and all sentient beings.;
Curators Comments:
"This, the oldest Nepalese image in the British Museum, is executed in the Gupta tradition that was well represented in the Nepal valley..." (Zwalf 1985,122); Zwalf 1985
This, the oldest Nepalese image in the British Museum, is executed in the Gupta tradition that was well represented in the Nepal valley, but the treatment of mass is more summary in ways that recall developments in Bihar during the pre-Pala period (c. AD 650-750). The inscription is also still in a Gupta character which seems a little later than many 7th-century examples. It names several donors who dedicate the merit from commissioning this image to the attainment of supreme knowledge (i.e. Buddhahood) by their teachers, kinsfolk and all sentient beings. The kneeling figure may be an undifferentiated donor carved to a common formula without reference to the specific commissioners of the piece.
Bib references: Zwalf 1985 / Buddhism: Art and Faith; Koezuka (1994) / Masterpieces of Buddhist and Hindu Art from the British Museum

Description: A figure of seated Maitreya (?) on chair; with the hands in mudra and the feet pendant. Made of cast bronze and gilded.;
Curators Comments:
Blurton, 1997:
The identification os this bronze is controversial. We know that as Buddhist teaching developed, the idea that figures in the evolving pantheon could be differentiated by their sitting positions or their hand gestures gained ground. On the other hand, the most usual feature in the identification of Maitreya is a small stupa located in the headdress, which here is not apparent. 
The Buddha usually wears a monastic robe, as here, a feature which often clearly reveals the body beneath it. This is a stylistic feature which, in India, reached back at least to the Gupta period. The Kathmandu valley is renowned, nol only for its high quality of metal-workmanship, but also for the extent to which Indian styles continued long after they had fallen out of fashion in the lowlands. The Gupta inheritance of this image, although many centuries later, is still apparent.; Zwalf 1985
The early concept of successive ages each ruled by a different Buddha recognised a future Buddha called Maitreya. Originally represented as an ornamented figure with a pot, he can later be indistinguishable from a Buddha making the preaching gesture and seated in the so-called European posture as on a chair. The identification of the seated and preaching Maitreya in Buddha form is clear when he has a ‘stūpa’ in his head-dress or on a flanking lotus. This image shows how the Gupta style persisted in Nepal.

Description: A standing figure of the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva, holding a vajra in his proper right hand in front of his chest and holding another in his left on side; wearing ornamental headdress and jewelries. Made of gilded copper.;
Curators Comments:
see von Schroeder 1981 for an extended bibliography.  This piece (identified there as Vajjrasatva) is dated to the 13th century by von Schroeder. (1981, 350).; Zwalf 1985
This superbly regal figure with ‘vajra’ and ‘ghaṇṭā’ follows an old Nepalese style of representing Bodhisattvas. The presence of Akṣobhya in the crown can be justified in the case of Vajrasattva as Supreme (Ādi) Buddha, since their connection is established in the texts. There is, however, also a Bodhisattva Vajrasattva, one of sixteen, connected with Akṣobhya. An identification as the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi seems textually unjustified, as Vajrapani is not reported in this form, although one late Nepalese image, holding both attributes in a somewhat different way, is claimed by Bhattacharyya as Vajrapāṇi and of Akṣobhya's 'family'.

Description: Two-armed Samvara (or Cakrasamvara)  (yi-dam) and Vajravarahi (in yab-yum on a lotus base) cast in a copper gilt set with coloured stones; under their feet the subjugated Hindu deities Kalaratri and Bhairava.;
Curators Comments:
For a two-armed Cakrasamvara in a 12th-13th century thangka, see Piotrovsky, Mikail Borisovich ed., Lost Empire of the Silk Road: Buddhist Art from Khara Khoto X-XIIIth Century (Milan: Electa & Thyssen-Bornemisza Foundation, 1993): p. 160, plate 27.; Zwalf 1985
A form of Samvara with one head and two arms is shown here in a vigorous posture, striding to the right and embracing his female partner. Both tread on Hindu gods, Bhairava, a form of Śiva, apparently holding a skull-cup, and his consort, Kālarātrī, with ritual knife and skull-cup; her emaciation, as goddess of death, is apparent from her pendulous breasts and angular arms and legs. Samvara holds his ‘vajra’ and ‘ghaṇṭā’ behind his consort's back, while she, one leg thrown over his left thigh above his lower garland of severed heads, holds a skull-cup and a broken ritual knife surmounted with the ‘vajra’ final.

Description: A figure of  Mañjuśrī seated on a lotus throne, holding a sword above his head in his right hand and a palm-leaf book in his left. Made of bronze with silver, copper and  turquoise inlay.;
Curators Comments:
Zwalf 1985
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī became popular in developed Buddhism and his cult spread to China and to Nepal, a country of which he is in a sense patron. Known also as prince or youth, he is the god of wisdom, and his usual attributes are the sword to cleave ignorance, and the oblong object in his left hand, the palm-leaf book equated with the text of the Perfection of Wisdom. The exceptional preservation of this image must be due to its export in antiquity to Tibet.

Description: Bronze seated figure of the Bodhisattva Guanyin, with both hands clasped around the left knee. Inscribed. Made of cast bronze.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: Back of shoulders Inscription language: Chinese Inscription script: Chinese Inscription quoted: 後至元已卯,曾□丘智淨抽資造七寶觀音,直頂奉,直至恭成佛道 Inscription translation: In the 5th year of Zhi Yuan, Zeng [unclear character] and the Monk Zhijing spared funds to make a Seven Treasures Bodhisattva Guanyin to be worshipped until they will sincerely achieve the goal of Buddhist practice. Inscription note: The inscription gives the date and records its offering by a monk, Zhijing, in his search for enlightenment.;
Curators Comments:
Rawson 1992:
The Mongol dynasty, the Yuan (1279-1368), patronised foreigners in the search for orthodox teachings in all aspects of government. Religion, particularly Buddhism, was an aspect of good government. The Mongols are said to have employed sculptors from Nepal, who introduced Nepalese and Tibetan forms of architecture and sculpture. The heavy sculptures of the Song dynasty were supplemented by a new and more elegant figure style, as can be seen in this bronze seateed Bodhisattva. The deeply curved body and lightly flowing drapery provide a sense of movement missing from earlier sculptures. Indeed, the contrast is evident in the difference in form and atmosphere in BM 1985.0726.1.

The inscriptions on the metal base document how the figure of Ugracaṇḍā was donated to the temple of Viśvakarmā by a series of individuals. The inscription on the left side, firstly, mentions Ruvuchuriṃ Tamrakar and his son Jayachuriṃ as donors. The top line of the inscription mentions the donors Kṛṣṇadeva Tamrakar and his brother Lakṣmīdhar (written as Rakṣmidhla). The second portion of the top line calls for an inscrease of wealth and offspring. Finally, the inscription on the right side mentions that 10 people shared in the donation to Viśvakarmā.

Description:
Lama (bla ma). Portrait figure of the renowned Sakya Master Drakpa Gyeltsen  (grags pa rgyal mtshan, 1147-1216)  holding a bell (ghanta) and sceptre (vajra); he is bearded and wears a robe incised scroll-work and auspicious Buddhist emblems. Cast in bronze; inlaid with silver and copper; incised with inscriptions on the double lotus base.
Along with his father Sachen Kunga Nyingpo (sa chen kun dga' snying po, 1092-1158) and his elder brother Sonam Tsemo (bsod nams rtse mo, 1142-1182), Drakpa Gyeltsen was one of the so called Sakya Patriarchs of the Sakya Religious Order, who were lay buddhist masters. He was a learned lama and Abbot of the Sakya Monastery, i.e. 'Sakya throne holder', for forty-three years, untill his death. He is portrayed wearing a elaborate dress, decorated with motifs of peonies and auspicious symbols. He performs the 'great embrace' (vajrahumkara) gesture, holding the vajra and the bell, his main attributes. He seats cross-legged on a double-lotus base.;

Description: Medium format slide (colour); 6x6; the sadhus are bathing in the Bagmati River. Pilgrims can be seen  in the background.;
Dimensions: 7.00 centimetres with frame ;  5.50 centimetres without frame ;  7.00 centimetres with frame ;  5.50 centimetres without frame ;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: front of frame Inscription note: Numbers handwritten by Hartsuiker.;
Curators Comments:
The Bagmati River flowing through the temple-complex of Pashupatinath near Khatmandu, Nepal, is a tributary of the Ganges. ‘Pashupati’ is one of the ancient names of Shiva, meaning ‘Lord of the Beasts’. One of the twelve jyotir-lingas (i.e ‘pillars of light’; self-created—not by human hands) is situated here, its origin shrouded in the mythological past. Evidently, this is a very holy spot. Especially for Shaiva babas, many of whom come here every year to celebrate Shivaratri (the night of Shiva). The water is too low for a dip, so the sadhu uses his kamandal (a gourd, called brahma-patra) to throw water over his body. The other baba just finished bathing and has rubbed fresh ashes on his body.
Of course, pilgrims and civilians bathe, and wash their clothes, here as well.
In the days leading up to Shivaratri night on 17-02-1988.

Description: Medium format slide (colour); 6x6; the sadhu, Naga baba Govindanand Puri sits in padmasana behind his dhuni, in front of a Shiva shrine, and wraps the chilam in a safi, preparatory to smoking charas. His jata is hanging loose; his face and body are covered in ash; around his neck he wears several rudraksh malas. A mala with large rudraksh beads (that he may use for japa) is lying in front of him, in line with two batteries, heating up in the sun; on the right is his jholi.;

Curators Comments:
The smoking of ganja (marihuana) or preferably charas (hashish) is an everyday ritual for many sadhus. Mixed with tobacco it is stuffed in a chilam (pipe) and lighted with a glowing coal from the dhuni. A damp piece of cloth—the safi—is wrapped around the lower end of the chilam. The safi serves the dual purpose of filtering the smoke and keeping the chilam clean (saf is ‘clean’), preventing any pollution by spittle, which is considered the most defiling bodily excretion. Playing it safe, most smokers use their own safi. Babas may use each other’s safi, but they would never lend it to non-sadhus, who, in their turn, discriminate against lower castes. 
Naga baba Govindanand Puri will stay, out in the open (and it’s freezing cold at night), for Shivaratri. This photograph was taken in the days leading up to Shivaratri night on 17-02-1988.

Description: Painting. Oil painting on canvas. The adoration of the Śālagrāma is shown in the middle of the picture. To the left, is Balakṛṣṇa holding the butter ball. On the right, a female figure holds a parasol over a central throne which suggests an aniconic reverence to Viṣṇu, also suggested by the large conch positioned centrally in the foreground. Other ritual objects typically used in 'puja' can be seen too: a copper water-pourer and a bell.;
Curators Comments:
Blurton 2006:
The circular black object that is garlanded and propped up on the seat of the throne is probably a 'salagram', an ammonite fossil. These circular stones, which occur in, and are collected from, the gorge of the Kali Gandaki river in western Nepal, are believed in India to be naturally occurring forms of the god Vishnu and, by extension, of Krishna, who for his devotees is not just the eighth incarnation of Vishnu but the supreme deity above all others. Thus, on the altars of many Bengali families the 'salagram' has pride of place at 'puja', rather than a metal or stone image. This seems to be in contradistinction to what is found in temples, where a metal image is more usual.
Bib references: Blurton 2006 / Bengali Myths; Mason 2009 / Kantha.  The Embroidered Quilts of Bengal

Curators Comments:
Descriptive text taken from Tantra: Enlightenment to Revolution (I. Ramos), draft of a manuscript accompanying an exhibition with the same working title planned for G35, Spring 2020.
Throughout the 1960s and 70s many European and American travellers embarked on the overland ‘Hippie Trail’ through Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, India and Nepal, the final destination for many (the trail was often referred to as the Road to Kathmandu). Perceived as a utopian haven surrounded by sacred Hindu and Buddhist monuments, lush valleys and mountains, the city was at the centre of Nepal’s ‘Tantric kingdom’ until the monarchy was dissolved by Maoists in 2008. Before 1973 cannabis was sold legally in Kathmandu, and one of the most well-known businesses was the Eden Hashish Centre owned by D.D. Sharma in Basantpur. Posters advertising the Centre to tourists featured images of deities, including this 1960s example, aptly depicting the intoxicated Shiva with his penchant for bhang. The Centre’s slogan, ‘Let us take higher’, appears below the image inviting people to ‘come visit us any time for all your hashish needs.’ Customers could purchase ‘temple balls’ at the Centre and consume them in the Heavenly Pleasure Room at Sharma’s nearby Eden Hotel.
Exhibition history: Sep 2020 - Jan 2021, BM, Room 35, "Tantra: enlightenment to revolution"

Dimensions: 68.50 centimetres Mounted ;  50.60 centimetres;  51.00 centimetres Mounted ;  36.20 centimetres;
Curators Comments:
Descriptive text taken from Tantra: Enlightenment to Revolution (I. Ramos), draft of a manuscript accompanying an exhibition with the same working title planned for G35, Spring 2020.
A 1967 poster advertises the ‘Gathering of the Tribes for a Human Be-In’ festival in San Francisco (January 14th), which took place at Golden Gate Park and is regarded as one of the most consciousness-raising events of the decade in its call to promote communal living, ecological awareness, critique of the prevailing socio-political order, engagement with Asian religious traditions including Tantric Hinduism and Buddhism and the use of psychedelic drugs for the purpose of inducing altered states of consciousness. Yoga and meditation were heralded as self-transformative practices that could inspire revolutionary minds to challenge and question capitalist structures. The bottom of the poster reads: ‘Bring food to share, bring flowers, beads, costumes, feathers, bells, cymbals, flags,’ encapsulating the spirit of the bohemian Hippie movement which was lent impetus by the festival. The poster depicts one of the most iconic images of that decade, designed by Stanley Mouse and Alton Kelley (the poster is signed by both of them) – a photographic portrait taken in Nepal by the artist Casey Sonnabend of a yogi with long dreadlocks. A pyramidal shape is superimposed over his head and shoulders and a third eye surrounded by rays of light is included above his brow. This third eye alludes not only to the Indian eye of awakening, which provides enlightened insight beyond ordinary perception, but also to the Eye of Providence or all-seeing eye of God, a Christian symbol enclosed by a triangle.  Yogis, with their purported supernormal abilities and transcendence of ego and materialism, captured the popular imagination in the West as counter-cultural role models. The poster lists the special guest speakers and performers at the festival, including the Beat poet Allen Ginsberg who chanted ‘Om’ on stage, the seed of all mantras. Ginsberg’s travels around India between 1962-3 convinced him that Tantra could teach American society how to unlearn oppressive, puritanical and moralistic middle-class principles. His meetings with yogis, many of whom consumed bhang or cannabis as part of their practice, had a profound effect on him and he recorded his own experience of smoking with them in his journals.

Description: Cotton inlay-patterned woven shawl (pachaura) in light pink, orange, dark gold, light gold, pale yellow and purple on dark pink ground; supplementary weft and inlay broken lozenge designs with stripes towards either end; black tassels at both ends.;
Curators Comments:
Text from Eth Doc1853: The shawl encompasses traditional and new designs in an unusually wide variety of colours.
     The work of the cotton inlay weavers in the Koshi Hills of east Nepal was featured in the Museum of Mankind's Himalayan Rainbow exhibition in 1983/84.  This showed the traditional method of weaving as well as the first results of a cottage industry development programme (KHARDEP: Koshi Hill Area Rural Development Programme) undertaken by His Majesty's government of Nepal with the support of the Overseas Development Administration.  The programme included agriculture, forestry, irrigation, health, education, roads and cottage industries.  His Majesty's government has given much attention to the development of cottage crafts, especially in the rural areas, the home of 95% of the population of 17 m.  In support of this and particularly in view of the very limited potential in the mountainous areas for expanding agriculture for small farmers, the aim of the cottage industry programme was to create off-farm employment which could help to provide additional income for the households of the Koshi Hill area.  The aim had been to build on traditional skills and ensure that the individual weaver continued to make the decisions about pattern and designs and to encourage creativity.  Assistance from 1981-85 consisted mainly of help with the supply of raw materials and labour-saving devices (e.g. warping mill, reeds and shuttles), workshops, product development and marketing.  The financial aid of KHARDEP terminated in 1985 but the 60-80 weavers in the project continued to weave traidtional as well as new colour combinations and patterns.
     There is a nucleus of skilled craftworkers and weavers in the Terhathum, Dhankuta and Ankhisalla districts, and an expanding market in Nepal for dhaka and allo cloth, traditional embroidery, and the baskets which are the specialties of the area.  Outlets also exist in the UK, including Liberty's. [from: 'The Mahaguthi Project, East Nepal, written by the International Trust for Nature Conservation, c. 1990.]

Description: A thangka of a maṇḍala at the centre of which is Vasudhara (goddess of abundance and consort of Jambhala). The following sacred figures are depicted in this painting: Buddha Ratnasambhava, goddess Ila, Jambhala, the Buddha, Dhyani Buddhas, Sucandra, Manjusri, Vajracarya performing the homa sacrifice. Painting on cloth. Inscribed.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: lower border Inscription translation: a dated dedication;
Curators Comments:
Zwalf 1985
A painted ‘maṇḍala’, a diagram within which a principal deity is enclosed with his or her entourage or emanations, is physically one or more squares representing a sacred building which has gateways at the cardinal points. The centre is occupied by the deity being invoked; the squares are enclosed in a circle demarcating the sacred area. ‘Maṇḍalas’ are used for initiations, meditation and rites of a magical character.
A ‘maṇḍala’ of Vasudhārā is used for a ritual of material advantage. The inner building of this ‘maṇḍala’ consists of three concentric squares with gateways. In the centre the large figure of the six-armed Vasudhārā makes her usual gestures (cf. no. 164): only the empty hand in her lap should hold a pot of plenty. Above is her 'parent' Buddha Ratnasambhava, 'the jewel-born', and below the goddess Ilā, and she is flanked by Bodhisattvas while spirits pour jewels from above. The blue deity at her bottom right is Jambhala, god of riches, and corresponding to him on the left a serpent king. In the second and outer squares are protector spirits. The area immediately outside the circle contains Ratnasambhava, Bodhisattvas and auspicious symbols, and framing the painting almost entirely are rows of scenes. In the top centre are the five Dhyāni Buddhas. Other scenes are devoted to the story of Sucandra and his son who stole bricks from a ‘stūpa’ with unhappy results. The theft is shown in the middle section of the single strip on the bottom left-hand side. The Buddha, propitiated by Sucandra, recommends the worship of Vasudhārā (she is seen emerging from a flower in the strip below the top right-hand corner). Sucandra was restored to his former wealth.
At the bottom of the painting above the dated dedication is the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. He is flanked by scenes showing a horse and an elephant, each carrying auspicious symbols, perhaps together representing with the other figures the Universal Monarch and his attributes. Beside them are worshippers. The ‘homa’, or fire sacrifice, is being performed on the left by a Vajrācārya wearing his helmet and pouring ghee into the fire; male and female worshippers kneel on both sides.

Description: Contemporary Bhutanese thangka (painting on fabric) depicting the Tantric Buddhist goddess Vajrayogini by Dasho Karma Ura;
Curators Comments: This Bhutanese thangka (painting on fabric) depicting the Tantric Buddhist goddess Vajrayogini was painted by Dasho Karma Ura (b. 1961) between September 2020 and March 2021 as a special commission for the British Museum. Vajrayogini is a meditational deity whose popularity flourished in India between the 10th and 12th centuries, and whose role assumed particular importance in the Himalayan regions of Tibet, Nepal and Bhutan. The contemporary thangka complements an existing collection of historical representations of Vajrayogini, highlighting both the continuity of artistic traditions in the region (influenced by Tibetan schools of painting) and Vajrayogini’s lasting importance in contemporary Tantric Buddhist practice. The commission emerged out of a collaboration with the Centre for Bhutan Studies in Thimphu. Karma Ura (President of the Centre) is a highly established artist and has completed numerous commissions for Bhutan’s royal family, some of which can be seen in Dochula Temple near Thimphu. He was awarded the ancient title of distinction, Dasho, by His Majesty the Fourth King in December 2006, for his dedicated service to the country. In 2010, he was bestowed the honour of Druk Khorlo (Wheel of Dragon Kingdom) by His Majesty the King for his contributions to literature and fine arts.

Description: A bronze Vajra or ritual thunderbolt, paired with the ghanta (bell) 1948,0716.11.a, together stored in a red leather covered container.;
Curators Comments:
Zwalf 1985
The ‘vajra’ and ‘ghaṇṭā’ were the most important ritual implements of Vajrayāna Buddhism. The ‘vajra’, symbolising the unbreakable Absolute, hardly survives as a ritual object from Buddhist India but is found in Indonesia, Nepal, Tibet and Japan. Paired with the bell, it symbolised compassion or the 'male' skill in means for salvation; the bell was the symbol of supreme knowledge seen as female. Together they constituted a unity of coefficients for salvation. Held in the right and left hands respectively to make elaborate ritual movements, they are also the attributes of many deities.

Franks, Esq. 29 March 1893. (Betts).'

Acq name (previous): Donated by: Sir Augustus Wollaston Franks
Acq notes (acq): As,+.5995 to 6004 come from Nepal; they were given by A W Franks on 29 March 1893, and recorded as coming from 'Betts', who can be identified as a government official, Lester Betts. (see this biography). Another part of the same collection (apparently the 'religious' material) from Nepal and Tibet was registered as 1893,0317, of which the numbers run from 1 to 75 but with many gaps. Lester Betts had made the collection recently in Nepal and Tibet.

Description: A polished stone axe or celt with a rounded blade end and short body ending in a slightly angled foot. Blade unbevelled.;
Curators Comments: The collector is said to have travelled widely in the old Indian Empire during his military service and we have only the recollections of his son and grandson to substantiate the findspot they report for these pieces. They are adamant in this recollection, however, and it is reasonable to record it (ie Western Nepal) as the best provenance we have for the axes/celts. Title: Tibetan Nobleman
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription quoted: Lily Eversdyk Smulders-1959. Tibetan Nobleman in government-service in Offial Attire and Hairdo-;
Curators Comments:
Lily Eversdijk-Smulders (1903-1994), portrait painter and lawyer.
She obtained her degree of Doctor of Law at the University of Leiden, Holland. After few years as a lawyer, she decided to dedicate herself to the arts. She travelled to Bali, Japan, China, all of West Asia, the Sahara desert, Central Africa, India and South America. She always travelled alone and mingled with the crowd in the countries she visited.
Through a curious set of circumstances, was adopted as a daughter by a Tibetan Redcap lama. Her book, Enigmatic Tibet published by Vantage Press Inc. New York, 1971, tells the story.
Condition: Both drawing and paper are in good condition, the drawing is kept in a polyester pocket and housed in a box.

Description: A polished stone axe with beaked blade and rounded edge.;
Curators Comments: The collector travelled widely in the old Indian Empire and we have only the recollections of his son and grandson to substantiate the findspot they report for these pieces. Title: Tibetan Nomad
Description:
Drawing; from a collection of sixty-one: “Tibetan Nomad”; adult male "Chaydor" playing a lute. Patan, Nepal, April 14th, 1961.
Chalk and crayon.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription quoted: Tibetan Nomad. Lily Eversdyk Smulders;
Curators Comments:
Lily Eversdijk-Smulders (1903-1994), portrait painter and lawyer.
She obtained her degree of Doctor of Law at the University of Leiden, Holland. After few years as a lawyer, she decided to dedicate herself to the arts. She travelled to Bali, Japan, China, all of West Asia, the Sahara desert, Central Africa, India and South America. She always travelled alone and mingled with the crowd in the countries she visited.
Through a curious set of circumstances, was adopted as a daughter by a Tibetan Redcap lama. Her book, Enigmatic Tibet published by Vantage Press Inc. New York, 1971, tells the story.
Condition: Both drawing and paper are in good condition, the drawing is kept in a polyester pocket and housed in a box.

Description: One from a collection of 234 neolithic stone tools.;
Curators Comments:
The collector is said to have travelled widely in the old Indian Empire during his wartime military service. We we have only the recollections of his son and grandson of conversations with Mr Peacey, to substantiate the findspot they report for these pieces. They are adamant in this recollection, however, and it is reasonable to record it as the best provenance (ie Western Nepal) we have for the axes/celts. 
It is most likely that this large hoard of neolithic stone axes, etc, was found originally, gathered together and collected at one place, possibly a country shrine of some kind and an indication that they may have been under worship or that they were objects venerated in some way.
Condition: Many of these tools have on their surfaces traces of the reddening that was evident in the group acquired earlier this year (2005.1-13.1-80). This substance has yet to be identified precisely.
Acq name (finding): Funded by: Brooke Sewell Permanent Fund
Acq notes (acq): Said to have been collected in western Nepal by Mr Walter Peacey (see Acq biography) during his military service in wartime India, these objects were nearly lost when he forgot the kit bag containing them at Leeds railway station, on his return from the East. They were returned to him a month later. They remained in his possession until his death in 1981 and have been sold to the Museum by his grandson, Mr Mark Peacey. The first part of this group (80 objects) came to the BM in January 2005 and is registered as 2005.1-13.1-80. The second part of this collection (234 objects) was found by the Peacey family in December of 2005 in another attic. It  came to the BM in December 2005 as the final part of this large (ie now some 314 objects) collection.

The first part of this group (80 objects) came to the BM in January 2005 and is registered as 2005.1-13.1-80. The second part of this collection (234 objects) was found by the Peacey family in December of 2005 in another attic. It  came to the BM in December 2005 as the final part of this large (ie now some 314 objects) collection.

The first part of this group (80 objects) came to the BM in January 2005 and is registered as 2005.1-13.1-80. The second part of this collection (234 objects) was found by the Peacey family in December of 2005 in another attic. It  came to the BM in December 2005 as the final part of this large (ie now some 314 objects) collection.

Description: One from a collection of 234 neolithic stone tools.;
Curators Comments:
The collector is said to have travelled widely in the old Indian Empire during his wartime military service. We we have only the recollections of his son and grandson of conversations with Mr Peacey, to substantiate the findspot they report for these pieces. They are adamant in this recollection, however, and it is reasonable to record it as the best provenance (ie Western Nepal) we have for the axes/celts. 
It is most likely that this large hoard of neolithic stone axes, etc, was found originally, gathered together and collected at one place, possibly a country shrine of some kind and an indication that they may have been under worship or that they were objects venerated in some way.
Some bear traces of red matter on their surfaces, many appear to have been fire blackened.
Condition: Many of these tools have on their surfaces traces of the reddening that was evident in the group acquired earlier this year (2005.1-13.1-80). This substance has yet to be identified precisely.

Description: A crudely fashioned and damaged ground stone axe or celt with a rounded blade end and a rectangular-sectioned body. Blade slightly bevelled on one side. Body broken off near the butt end though this may simply be a crudely made foot.;
Dimensions: 9.30 centimetres maximum ;  1.60 centimetres;  6.40 centimetres at blade ;
Curators Comments:
The collector is said to have travelled widely in the old Indian Empire during his military service and we have only the recollections of his son and grandson to substantiate the findspot they report for these pieces. They are adamant in this recollection, however, and it is reasonable to record it (ie Western Nepal) as the best provenance we have for the axes/celts. They have a more eastern look to me (JRK) than western and it is quite possible that they found their source in upper Burma or the eastern Himalayas.
This celt, as many others in this group, appears to be covered, at least in part, with a dark, slightly sticky surface coating not yet identified as any particular substance. Occasional specimens bear traces of red material on their surfaces.

Title: Tibetaans Meisje
Description:
Drawing; from a collection of sixty-one: "Tibetaans Meisje". Sherab Unzang; the taylor's daughter;  young adult female wearing red and grey costume with beaded necklace and decorated fur hat. Patan, Nepal, April 10th, 1961.
Chalk and crayon.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription quoted: Lily Eversdyk Smulders: Tibetaans Meisje;
Curators Comments:
Lily Eversdijk-Smulders (1903-1994), portrait painter and lawyer.
She obtained her degree of Doctor of Law at the University of Leiden, Holland. After few years as a lawyer, she decided to dedicate herself to the arts. She travelled to Bali, Japan, China, all of West Asia, the Sahara desert, Central Africa, India and South America. She always travelled alone and mingled with the crowd in the countries she visited.
Through a curious set of circumstances, was adopted as a daughter by a Tibetan Redcap lama. Her book, Enigmatic Tibet published by Vantage Press Inc. New York, 1971, tells the story.
Condition: Both drawing and paper are in good condition, the drawing is kept in a polyester pocket and housed in a box.
Acq name (acq): Donated by: Dr Lily Eversdijk-Smulders;  Donated through: Ms Ella Andriesse
Acq name (previous): Donated by: Dr Lily Eversdijk-Smulders;  Donated through: Ms Ella Andriesse
Acq notes (acq): The collection of sixty-one drawings from Asia, Africa and South America, were left to the department in the artist's will and after her death in 1994, they were presented  to the BM on 24th January 1995 by Ms Ella Andriesse.

Drawing; from a collection of sixty-one: Tibetan city dweller; wearing costume decorated fur hat, ear-rings, necklace and a triple blade ritual dagger. Patan, Nepal, April 3rd, 1961.
Chalk and crayon.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription quoted: Lily Eversdyk Smulders;
Curators Comments:
Lily Eversdijk-Smulders (1903-1994), portrait painter and lawyer.
She obtained her degree of Doctor of Law at the University of Leiden, Holland. After few years as a lawyer, she decided to dedicate herself to the arts. She travelled to Bali, Japan, China, all of West Asia, the Sahara desert, Central Africa, India and South America. She always travelled alone and mingled with the crowd in the countries she visited.
Through a curious set of circumstances, was adopted as a daughter by a Tibetan Redcap lama. Her book, Enigmatic Tibet published by Vantage Press Inc. New York, 1971, tells the story.

Description: A polished celt in mottled and banded stone with a lenticular section, a beaked rounded blade without bevelling, a short body and a roughly ground distinctly angled foot. Small quantities of a reddish material appear to adhere to rough areas of the body surface (esp. the foot).;
Curators Comments:
The collector is said to have travelled widely in the old Indian Empire during his military service and we have only the recollections of his son and grandson to substantiate the findspot they report for these pieces. They are adamant in this recollection, however, and it is reasonable to record it (ie Western Nepal) as the best provenance we have for the celts/axes. 
This celt, as many others in this group, appears to be covered, at least in part, with a dark, slightly sticky surface coating, sometimes with red inclusions not yet identified as any particular substance.
Acq name (finding): Funded by: Brooke Sewell Permanent Fund
Acq notes (acq): Collected in western Nepal by Mr Walter Peacey, these objects were nearly lost when he forgot the kit bag containing them at Leeds railway station on his return from the East. They were returned to him a month later. They remained in his possession until his death in 1981 and have been sold to the Museum by his grandson, Mr Mark Peacey.

Description: A crudely fashioned and damaged ground stone axe or celt with a rounded blade end and a rectangular-sectioned body. Blade slightly bevelled on one side. Body broken off near the butt end though this may simply be a crudely made foot. Traces of red matter on both surfaces.;
Dimensions: 9.30 centimetres maximum ;  1.60 centimetres;  6.40 centimetres at blade ;
Curators Comments:
The collector is said to have travelled widely in the old Indian Empire during his military service and we have only the recollections of his son and grandson to substantiate the findspot they report for these pieces. They are adamant in this recollection, however, and it is reasonable to record it (ie Western Nepal) as the best provenance we have for the axes/celts. They have a more eastern look to me (JRK) than western and it is quite possible that they found their source in upper Burma or the eastern Himalayas.
This celt, as many others in this group, appears to be covered, at least in part, with a dark, slightly sticky surface coating not yet identified as any particular substance. Occasional specimens bear traces of red material on their surfaces.

Description: Small format slide (colour); 35mm colour negative; Lakshmi Narayana Giri.;
Dimensions: 5.00 centimetres with frame ;  2.40 centimetres without frame ;  5.00 centimetres with frame ;  3.50 centimetres without frame ;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: front of frame Inscription note: Numbers handwritten by Hartsuiker.;
Curators Comments:
Lakshmi Narayana Giri, dignified in his simplicity and poverty, obeying the ascetic precept of possessing no more than the absolute necessities, resides temporarily in front of a Shiva shrine at Pashupatinath in Nepal, where he has come to celebrate the yearly festival of Shivaratri. He wears a rudraksh mala around the neck; a worn aluminum kamandal is standing on the left.
In the days leading up to Shivaratri night on 17-02-1988.
Narayana is another name of Lord Vishnu, and means “Refuge of Man”.
This slide is part of the Hartsuiker Archive of 1900 colour slides, consisting of 300 in 6x6 format and 1600 35mm slides. This archive  documents Indian mendicants or Sadhus, mostly Hindu, but including some Jain practitioners, in the later 20th century in northern India. The images were taken by Dolf Hartsuiker over many years, from the 1970s onwards.
Hartsuiker rating: 6
Bib references: Hartsuiker 1993 / Sadhus: Holy Men of India

Description: Illustrated wall calendar titled “Nepalese Art & Culture” for the year 1986, printed in black ink on thin off-white paper. The calendar consists of multiple pages, each combining monthly date grids with vignette-style illustrations depicting scenes of everyday life, religious architecture, festivals, labour, and landscapes associated with Nepalese culture. The imagery includes women drawing water at a communal well, agricultural labourers working in terraced landscapes, festival processions with musicians and chariots, mountain scenery with seated figures, temple complexes and shrines, domestic craft production, and urban scenes with porters carrying goods. Architectural forms such as pagoda temples, stupas, shrines, palace courtyards, and Newar-style buildings appear throughout the composition. The pages are printed in a documentary and illustrative style. Woodblock print.;
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: upper margin and cover page Inscription language: English Inscription script: Roman Inscription quoted: NEPALESE ART & CULTURE;
Subjects: calendar (1986 accompanied by Vikram Samvat date)

Description: Register 1954: Wooden figurine of a two-wheeled cart drawn by two horses; with headless human figurine sitting on top of cart.;
Curators Comments:
Register 1954:
Nepal.
The female figures were offerings by women making a request at a shrine or temple, the others may be toys. 
All were found in temples or old houses in Kathmandu or Patan. 
They were made by the non-mongoloid Nawar of the Kathmandu Valley and date from before or not long after the Gurkha conquest c. 1840.
These figurines are new being reproduced and made to look old artificially.
(The above information, supplied by donor, is difficult to reconcile with Nepalese history.)

A group of dandi sannyasis who are carrying the ekdanda in long orange bags.
In the days leading up to Shivaratri night on 17-02-1988.
Carrying this particular staff, the ekdanda, is the prerogative of sannyasis belonging to the Brahmin caste. It is a branch from the vainu tree—from which also Krishna’s magic flute is fashioned. It has a little flag attached to it, called parashu mudra, i.e. ‘symbol of the battle-ax’, and signifies the willingness to teach others. The white piece of cloth lower down is called Lakshmi patt, and is used for puja to Lord Vishnu. The number of joints (ghat) on the staff varies from 8 to 14, and the more the better. It is usually carried in a bag (with room for the flag) to prevent it from becoming polluted. It can be shown openly when carrying out puja or when cleaning it with holy water.
Strangely enough, this is all Vaishnava terminology and symbolism, whereas the ekdanda is carried by Shaivas.

Dimensions: 5.00 centimetres with frame ;  2.40 centimetres without frame ;  5.00 centimetres with frame ;  3.50 centimetres without frame ;

Gorakhnathis of the kanphata subsect sit in the courtyard of the Gorakhnath temple in Pashupatinath. The baba in the centre with the many malas one of sphatik (crystal), and shaili (mala with whistle) around his neck, the small chimta with bells in his left hand, and silver chimta in the right hand, is Lakshman Nath. His jholi, adorned with a red dhvaja (banner), is hanging on his right shoulder. His tilak consist of ash over the forehead and a red bindu dot in the centre.
The baba on the left, Tiloki Nath, wears an ivory kundal, a distinct kanphata ‘accessory’, in his right ear. 
The baba on the right is crumbling charas in his hand to prepare a chilam. He wears a glass kundal in the left ear. A brass kamandal is standing in front of him.
In the days leading up to Shivaratri night on 17-02-1988.
One section of the Goraknathi Yogis goes by the name of Kanphatas—i.e. ‘split ears’—which refers to their practice of piercing the central portion of the ears and inserting large circular earrings during a second initiation. The cartilage of the ear is perforated with a double-edged knife, and provisional clay rings are put in place. The operation, it is said, confers immediate enlightenment. When the wounds have healed, the clay rings are replaced by rings made of ‘powerful’ materials, such as rhinoceros-horn, ivory, semi-precious stone, and even airplane-glass.
Another name for the kundal is darshani, referring to the darshan (“vision”) of the deity made possible by it’s use.
Goraknathis are Shaivas, and indeed Shiva himself is often portrayed with large earrings.
The Gorakhnathis usually add the suffix ‘Nath’ (‘Master’) to their name, which is a title of Shiva, suggesting the possession of supernatural powers.

Description: Large bronze spittoon with flaring lip; the globular body gadrooned with lotus petals above and below this central part of the vessel.  The spreading foot is also decorated with an elementary relief of lotus petals.  The heavily decorated sections of the vessel contrast with those parts left plain, producing a pleasing and handsome effect.;
Production place: Made in: Nepal (On stylistic grounds almost certainly made by Newari metalsmiths in the Kathmandu valley)
Acq name (acq): Donated by: Simon Digby Memorial Charity (Part of a group of metalwork from the collection of the late Simon Digby, given by the SD Charity.)
Acq name (previous): Donated by: Simon Digby Memorial Charity (Part of a group of metalwork from the collection of the late Simon Digby, given by the SD Charity.)
Acq notes (acq): From the estate of Professor Simon Digby (1932-2010), either collected by him or acquired by his parents (his father was Chief Justice of the central provinces in Nagpur, India) or by his grandparents (stationed in Bombay at the turn of the 19th/20th century). Other members of his family were stationed in Myanmar (Burma).

Description: Engraved ivory circular magical plaque (yantra). On face: successive concentric circles contain the nine digits, eight trigrams and twelve figures of the zodiac, the Tibetan 'Om mani padme hum' formula, together with symbols for the days of the week. All enclosed in a fret border. On the reverse: the 'visvavajra' in a scalloped field; small drilled concentric circles outside.;
Bib references: Neumark 1991 / Selected Acquisitions: May to July
Subjects: zodiac; devil/demon; eight days of the week

Title: The modern idol jaggernaut.; The Grand Master or Adventures of Qui Hi? In Hindostan a Hudibranstic poem in eight cantos by quiz.
Producer name: Print made by: Thomas Rowlandson;  Published by: Thomas Tegg
Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription quoted: Lettered with title, artist's name and publishing details:  'Rowlandson sc. Quiz. fecit. / London, Published by T Tegg, No 111 Cheapside, Oct 1, 1815.';
Curators Comments:
(Description and comment from M. Dorothy George, 'Catalogue of Political and Personal Satires in the British Museum', IX, 1949)
An attack on the policy of Hastings directed especially against the Nepal war (see Fortescue, 'Hist. of the British Army', xi. 120 ff.): the Gurkhas had been raiding British India and killing or capturing the garrisons of small frontier stations; war was therefore declared in Nov. 1814; after reverses the British were successful, cf. No. 12729. For the Bishop of Calcutta see No. 12719.
(Supplementary information)
For the background of the series, see BM Sat No. 12718  (British Library,  C.59.f.11).
Bib references: BM Satires / Catalogue of Political and Personal Satires in the Department of Prints and Drawings in the British Museum
Assoc name: Associated with: Thomas Fanshaw Middleton, Bishop of Calcutta
